The lines in the Chronicle's voice are our own renderings of the Annales Bertiniani and Fuldenses for 834 to 837; nothing is quoted from a modern translation. Every card has an art.<card id> entry for the artist, and every ending an art.chain_dorestad_834.ending.<name>.

entries.text: Sails in Frisia
A fisherman from the outer coast has rowed two days to sell nothing. He has seen a fleet of the Danes come in among the islands, and smoke behind it.
Long ships, low, with the shields along the side. I stopped counting at thirty because I had started to row. There was smoke on two terps before I lost the land.
There used to be a fire kept ready on the dune and a count's man to light it. Since the emperor's sons took the emperor, the count's men have had other fires to see to.
They did not stay to rob fishermen. They were asking the way. A fleet that asks the way is going to a place, and there is one place up that river worth forty ships.
Nobody on the dams has heard it. A cask of wine is being argued over two berths down, at some length.
He says their swords were good ones. You sold good ones north, once. You do not ask him about the marks.
Take his word to the dams at Dorestad, now, as he gave it
Give him ale and bread and ask it all twice: how many, how laden, which mouth. Then carry it
Finish your business first. Frisia is wide, and fishermen see fleets every spring
You cast off within the hour with a fisherman's word and nothing to hang it on: many ships, some smoke. It is what you have. The dams are a day away.

The second telling is better than the first. Forty hulls or near it, riding light, so they have not filled them yet. They lay in the Vlie on the Thursday. A man could swear to that, and you may have to.
You finish your selling. It was a fair price. The fisherman tells the next boat, and the one after, and by the time you come home his story will be there before you, a little larger.
A fisherman's story
An hour's walk of open bank, a storehouse on every dam, and not so much as a ditch between the river and the richest market in the north. The dams are busy with the summer.
The word reached the dams without you, by a herring boat, two days ago. It has been well laughed at since.
The emperor has been put down by his sons and set up again since last harvest, and one son is still in the field. If I send to say a fisherman saw ships, who do you think will read it?
Forty. Riding light. In the Vlie on the Thursday. That is not a fisherman's story, that is a count. Say it again slowly and I will have it cut on a stick.
I have buried my silver twice in my life and dug it up once. I am not going looking for a spade because a man who sells eels has seen a sail.
In my father's day two hundred ships lay in Frisia and took a hundred pounds of silver, and not one of them came up this river. It is a long river. That is what it is for.
The rich will do as they please with a warning. The poor have no boats. If it is true, tell me today, because it takes me three days to move people who own nothing.
Swear to the king's agent: the count of ships, the day, the mouth they lay in
Cry it on the dams yourself, storehouse by storehouse
Tell the priest, and the women who know which of the poor are truly poor
Say no more. Buy three bolts from a nervous man at twenty pennies the bolt

He has it cut on a stick and sends a rider to Nijmegen, who will arrive too late and be believed afterwards. What matters is that the agent starts loading the king's own chest. The dams see that, and draw their own conclusion.

The first six laugh. The seventh is a woman who was a child on the coast in the year of the two hundred ships. She starts carrying her loom to the boat while you are still talking, and after that it goes down the bank faster than you can walk.

By the fourth dam they have a name for you. It is the name of a marsh bird that shouts before rain. Your own crew hear it and look at their feet. But you said it on every dam, and every dam will remember who did.
By evening the plate is in a farm cart under a load of reeds, and the women are going from door to door among the people who have nothing. Nobody on the dams notices. Nobody on the dams ever does.
He sells you three bolts at less than half their worth and thanks you for it. He has heard something and does not want to say what. Neither do you.
They are past Utrecht
A boy comes running down the bank road from the Utrecht side. They are past the bishop's town with their masts down, rowing. They will be here with the morning.
Half the dams are already empty. Boats have been going up the Lek for three days with looms, casks and children, and the farms inland are full of people who do not know how to milk.
The dams are full. Men who laughed four days ago are throwing cloth into boats that are already too deep, and shouting at each other for the way out.
I have twelve men and a dam four paces wide with water on both sides. They can only come at it from the front. Stand with me, or get out of my light.
I will not tell you it is likely. I will tell you I am too old and too fat to run, and my father built this.
Some of the blades coming up the river were forged on this river. You would know the marks, if you were close enough to read them.
The ships built here on the northern pattern are gone up the Lek already, every one. Nothing on this bank could row like that a lifetime ago.
Load what she will carry, take the neighbour's children, and run up the Lek tonight
Put the house's chest in the ground at De Heul and lie in the alders to watch
Stand on the dam head with Thiadlef's twelve men
You row all night against the stream with four children asleep on the cloth. At first light there is smoke behind you, a thin straight line of it, and one of the children asks whose house that is.

You count thirty-eight hulls from the alders. They work down the dams like men unloading a ship: no hurry, nothing dropped. Nobody looks at a graveyard. By night you have a riddle in your head about a thing that men dig for and hide again, and you know its answer.

A man foraging for pigs walks onto your hand. You leave your cloak and some skin with him and go through the marsh on your belly. The chest is still under its alder. So, for a week, is the feeling in your ribs.

They try the dam head once, find it costs two men, and go to the next dam, where it costs nothing. That is all. Thiadlef's store stands in a row of ash, and there is an arm ring on the planks that nobody comes back for. He tells you a riddle about a shield while his hands stop shaking.

It lasts as long as it takes to say a paternoster. You go into the ditch with a cut you do not feel until evening, and Thiadlef's men pull you out on the far side. The store burns. He says you stood there, and he says it to everyone.
What the fleet left
This year the heathen men came by Traiectum to Dorestad. Some of the people they killed, some they carried off, and a part of the place they burned.
Fewer are dead than might be. The boats that went up the Lek are coming back down full of people, and the ships went home lighter than they came for. They are saying on the dams whose word it was.
The plate of the upper church is back on its altar. It spent the week at Rijswijk in a farm cart, under reeds, and the people with no boats spent it in the same barn.
Your chest is where you left it, under an alder nobody would look at twice. You leave it there. It seems to like the place.
On your own plot the roof is gone from the store and the posts stand. The well is full of somebody's cooking pots.
They took my Hildswith off the bank road. Fourteen at Martinmas. A man saw her put into the third ship, alive and shouting. I am told that is good news.
They sell at Sliesthorp. Everyone knows it. Our own men trade there every summer, and when the bench comes out they look at their feet.
I have a dam head, forty paces of good oak post, and no husband to lie at it. I will not sell it this year. Ask me after the next one.
Tell Thiadlef you will ask after the girl at Sliesthorp
Give thirty pennies for shrouds and bread, and help carry
Buy what is offered behind the ale-house: a silver cup with a cross filed off it, ninety pennies
He nods once. He does not thank you, because you have not done it yet. He tells you what she was wearing, and that she counts things when she is frightened.
You carry eleven to the graves at De Heul before dark. The widow walks beside you for the last three and tells you each one's name and what he owed, so that somebody will know.
It is good silver and heavy. The man who sells it found it in the reeds, he says. The reeds have been generous this week. You wrap it in sailcloth and put it under the bottom boards.
Cloth with the seal still on it
On the landing a Dane sells Frisian cloth by the bolt, a Dorestad seal of lead still hanging from one of them. Behind the cloth, on a bench, sit the people who came in the same ships.
Good cloth. From the Rhine. I did not ask it how it came here, and it has not complained.
That one spins, and she has all her teeth. Her father is a rich man, she says. They all say it. Now and then it is true, and then I am glad I listened.
The third ship. Tell my father it was the third ship. I have a knot in my belt for every day, and I am not going to say how many.
King Horik had no part in it. When the emperor's house fights itself, men sail where they like, and a king cannot stand on every beach. I am told to say so to Franks. You will do.
The king has sent men to the emperor to say the fleets are not his. He also wants to know who killed his last messengers near Cologne. Both things are true. Only one of them is being asked about.
Two Dorestad skippers are selling wine thirty paces off. They have seen the bench. They are very busy with a cask.
Weigh out his price for the girl: a hundred and eighty pennies' weight
Bargain in his own tongue: a father's price, not a market's. A hundred and ten
Buy nothing. Drink with the king's man and ask when ships like those sail again

He weighs it twice on his own scales and once on yours. The girl gets up off the bench without being told, walks to your boat and sits down in the bow facing the water. She does not speak until the landing is out of sight. Then she asks whether the store burned.
In his own tongue he is a different man: a farmer with a debt and two daughters. He comes down seventy and throws in the belt she counted on. She is in your bow before the silver is in his bag.

He drinks your ale and tells you what any Dane could: they go when the sowing is done, they go where it was easy, and nothing on the Rhine was hard. They will go while the emperor's sons keep him busy. The girl watches you leave. You remember what she was wearing.
The third ship
Thiadlef is on his dam head before your rope is. He does not look at you at all until the girl is ashore.
I counted wrong by one. There was a day I slept through.
My father owed nobody on this river, and it took him forty years to arrange. I have owed you since you tied up. I do not intend it to last until dinner.
Here is the price twice over, counted. Or the price once and my order for Rhine wine, which is worth more if you can carry. Choose one and let me sleep.
My father would have asked what you want from me. I am asking what it cost. It is the only difference between us, and I am told it is an improvement.
Take what he counts out: the price twice over
Take the price once, and his order for ten casks of Rhine wine at half as much again
Take nothing. Tell him it was a neighbour's errand
He counts three hundred and sixty pennies onto a cask head and breathes out. You are quits, and he is plainly happier that way. The girl waves from the door of the store.
He counts out the price and cuts a tally for ten casks at half as much again as the market gives. A man does not order wine from someone he means to go on resenting.

He looks at you as if you had hit him. Next morning his own steersman is sitting on your gunwale with his sea chest: a man who can take a boat down the Lek by night with the mast down. Thiadlef has sent him for a season. He has not sent a message with him.
Earth or silver
The men who hold dam heads meet in the upper church, because it is the only roof big enough. There are three opinions, and each of them costs something.
The burned plots are roofed again with new thatch, very yellow. Everyone agrees that they will come again when the sowing is done. Nobody agrees on anything else.
This year the Northmen fell on Dorestad a second time and laid it waste. The emperor was much angered, and came to Aachen, and ordered guards set along the coasts.
The emperor has ordered the coast watched. He ordered it from Aachen. Aachen is nine days from the sea, and the order is travelling at the speed of a bishop.

A ditch and a bank from the old fort to the lower graves. A gate on the bank road. Twelve men who stay awake. Cologne has Roman walls. We have alder posts and a debt to God, and I know which I would rather stand behind.
They want silver. So next time we meet them at the river with silver on a cloth, and we keep our roofs. I have reckoned it. It is cheaper than earth, and nobody has to dig.
A third opinion is not spoken in church. It is a barge at the upstream end of the bank, loading a loom, with her head toward the IJssel.
The shipmen's common chest, a penny a voyage these forty years, votes its whole weight for the bank. Your share is the same, but the ditch will reach the river.
You know what the Danes say about it themselves: they go where it was easy. You say so. It is the only thing said all day that makes Thiadlef stop talking.
Put in the first share for the ditch and the bank: three hundred pennies
Start sending looms, scales and stock up the river to Daventre, a boatload a month
Do neither. Keep the stock short and the boat loaded, and sleep aboard from Pentecost to Lammas

Your silver goes into the priest's box with nine other houses' and the digging starts at the fort end on Monday. The king's agent, who cannot give leave for a bank, finds he can halve the toll of men who are too busy digging to trade. Leave is the palace's to give. Somebody should go to Nijmegen.

The first boatload goes up before the week is out: the big loom, the spare scales, the good cloth. On the dams they watch it go and say nothing to your face. The bench by the fire in the ale-house is a little narrower than it was.
You sell down to what one boat can lift in an hour, and move your bedding aboard. Most of the bank does the same. A market that sleeps in its boats still looks like a market from the river.
A gate on the king's ground
The palace on its hill above the Waal is half empty: the emperor is wherever his sons are. A clerk in the gatehouse has the keeping of what may and may not be built between here and the sea.
A bank I could overlook. A gate is another matter. A gate can be shut against a Dane, and it can be shut against a count. The palace likes to know which the builders had in mind.
You are the one who came with the count of ships in the first summer. It was written down. Very little that is true gets written down here, so we remember it when it does.
There is oak in the king's wood marked for a bridge that will not be built while the emperor's sons are talking to each other. Oak does not improve by lying.
The emperor forgives everyone, in time. He also arrives everywhere, in time. If your town means to be standing when he does, I would not wait for him.
Ask leave for the bank as the man who brought the warning in the first summer
Ask leave, with sixty pennies for the clerk's trouble
Ask nothing. Hear what has been ordered for the coast, and go home

He writes four lines, reads them to you in Latin and then in Frankish, and seals them with the count's seal. Six loads of the bridge oak go down to your boat. He says a gate built of the king's timber is the king's gate, and nobody can complain of that, least of all the king.
The sixty pennies vanish without a sound. The leave is four lines and a seal. He finds three loads of oak that were, on reflection, marked for nothing in particular.

What has been ordered is a watch on every river mouth, kept by the counts, who are all somewhere else with their men. You go home with that. A bank needs no leave to be dug, only to be defended afterwards in a court.
More than twice your hands

Sails under the land to the south, more than you can count on your hands twice, standing in for the mouth of the Maas. One of them hangs back, low in the water, and turns her head toward you. She has more oars than you have men.
Witla is behind those dunes: a market, a landing, a pilot's house. Beyond it is the Scheldt and the fort at Andoverpis. From there to the Lek is two days for men who row like that.
You have casks. We have a thirst and a long row ahead. Sell, and nobody on this water need be unhappy today.
Or run, if you like. We are not here for one small boat. But my rowers are bored, and I cannot answer for bored men.
Put about and run for the Lek with the word: they are on the Maas
Drop the sail, lie under the dunes and count them as they pass
Lie to, sell him two casks of ale at three times the price, and ask where they are bound

She chases for the length of a psalm and gives it up: a small boat with the wind free is not worth a bored crew's sweat. You are in the Lek two tides ahead of them, shouting it at every landing you pass.

She has you inside the hour. They take your bread, your water cask and a man's good cloak, laugh at the rest, and let you go. It is very nearly friendly. The word reaches the Lek a tide behind the smoke.
Mast down, in the lee of the dune, you count twenty-six. By evening there is smoke where Witla was, and by the next evening a second smoke further south. You know before any bishop does.

He pays in cut silver, three times the price, and does not haggle. Witla first, he says, then the fort on the Scheldt, then the Rhine as usual: he says 'as usual'. You have sixty pennies' weight more than you had, and it sits oddly in the bag.
The third summer
Nobody on the dams says 'if' any more. They say 'when they come', and name the feast. Wine and cloth go for whatever a man will give who is fool enough to keep them here.
This year the Northmen burned Andoverpis, and Witla, the market by the mouth of the Maas, and came again to Dorestad and into Frisia.
They remember whose boat came up the Lek shouting, two tides ahead of the smoke. There were very few on the bank road when the ships came, and nothing in the stores worth the row.
The ditch is dug from the fort to the bank road, and the bank is up to a man's chest. There is no gate. A bank with no gate is a hill with a road through it. I need the second share before Pentecost.
And the gate will be the king's oak, hung by the king's leave. I have read the four lines to every man who said it could not be done. Some of them asked me to read it again.
We talked about a bank, two summers ago. There was a great deal of agreement. I buried nineteen people on the strength of it.
I have the tribute chest half full already, from the houses that would sooner pay than dig. Silver on a cloth at the river. They will take it and go. They are merchants too, in their way.
Half your house is on the IJssel already. What is left here fits in two boatloads, and one of them is the cat.
A cask of Rhine wine that was sixty pennies at Easter is offered at twenty-five, on the dam, by a man who keeps looking downstream.
Pay the second share: the gate, the watch-house and twelve men's bread. Five hundred pennies
Take the rest up the river now, and leave the store to the mice
Fill the store while others empty theirs: a hundred and fifty pennies buys what was worth four hundred. Bury the chest first
Change nothing: stock short, boat loaded, one eye on the river

The gate is hung at midsummer: two leaves of oak, a bar a man can hardly lift, and a watch-house over it with a horn. Twelve men draw bread to stay awake in it. From the river the place looks, for the first time, like something that might answer back.

Two boatloads, and the door left open so that nobody need break it. Whatever you paid toward the bank stays in the bank. Thiadlef watches you cast off and says the IJssel is a fine river for people who like Saxons.

The fleet comes, takes what is easy, and does not come as far as your dam. At Martinmas every store on the bank is empty but yours, and the men who sold to you at twenty-five buy back at seventy. You do not smile until you are indoors.

They come before Lammas, and a full store is the first thing they find. What they cannot carry they burn. You watch it from the alders with the smell of your own wine in the smoke. The chest is in the ground. It is all of the house that is not ash.
You change nothing. When they come there is an hour's warning, your boat is loaded, and what burns of yours is a roof. It is not a way to grow rich. It is a way to be here next year.
The gate was shut

This year the heathen men took Walcheren and killed its count, and came up the river to Dorestad as in other years. There was a ditch there now, and a bank, and a gate on the bank road, and it was shut.

They lie two days below the lower graves, looking at it. A man rows up to shout that silver on a cloth would save trouble on both sides. The horn answers him. On the third tide they go down the river, and that evening there is no smoke.
I said silver was cheaper than earth. I was wrong by about the price of my roof, and I have stood on your bank for three nights to say so. Do not ask me to say it again.
The emperor is at Nijmegen, asking his counts why the coast was not kept. They are telling him it could not be done. I am to bring him one place where it was. He will want a name to go with it.
And it was done by his own leave, with his own oak in the gate. That will please him more than the bank does. He can say he ordered it.
He will ask who gave leave for a gate on his ground. I shall say the Danes did, three summers running. I think he will let that stand.
One thing more. A bank is twelve men awake every night from Pentecost to Lammas, for ever. Every house that built it owes a man and his bread. Yours too, and your son's.
Ask the emperor's writing: your house free of the tenth at Dorestad
Ask a seat among the seven who find judgment on the bank
You brought the first warning and you had his leave: let the agent name you at Nijmegen, and ask both

The writing comes down from Nijmegen within the month: your house and its heirs free of the tenth at Dorestad, which the emperor's own merchants pay. The dam heads repay your shares with a third over, fifteen hundred pennies, because a bank that worked is suddenly everybody's idea. The house owes the watch a man each summer.

At the next court you sit with the six who find judgment, on the bench nearest the door, where the newest man sits. The shares come back with interest, twelve hundred pennies, and the agent halves your toll for a year without being asked. The house owes the watch a man each summer.

The agent names you before the emperor, who is glad of one piece of good news and generous with it. The writing frees your house of the tenth; the court makes room on its bench; the bank repays you twice over, twenty-four hundred pennies. In the annals of that year it will say that tribute was taken at Walcheren. It will not say Dorestad. The house owes the watch a man each summer.
Weighed out on the dam head
This year the heathen men took Walcheren and killed its count, and took what tribute they chose. Then they came up the river to Dorestad and took tribute there in the same way.
The bank you paid toward stands to a man's chest and stops at the road. They walked through where the gate was going to be.
Silver now, by weight, and we go down on the ebb with nothing burned. We killed a count on the island eight days ago and a good Dane beside him. We have had enough work for one summer.
I told you. Silver on a cloth. Nobody dead, no roof gone. Ask me next year whether it was cheap, when they come back for the same again. Ask me quietly.
And I still owe you for the third ship. I have not forgotten it for one day. It is like a stone in a shoe.

The emperor has turned back from his road to Rome and is coming to Nijmegen in a rage. He will ask why the coast was not kept. Somebody will tell him the Frisians would not obey. Somebody always does.
There are people on the rowing benches of the nearest ship who are not rowers. Some of them have been there since the island. One or two have been there longer.
Advance three hundred pennies for the houses that cannot find their share, against their pledges
Carry the silver down to the ships yourself, and speak for the people on the benches
Pay your share, and take what Thiadlef has been waiting to offer since you brought his daughter home
Pay your share and no more, and carry bread and ale down the Lek by night to a town with no silver left

Your three hundred makes up the weight. By Michaelmas four of the houses you covered have not redeemed their pledges, and do not pretend they will: twelve bolts of cloth, eight casks of wine, and a dam head whose owner is going to his brother at Tiel. You have a berth of your own. You did not much like the way you came by it.

You stand in the mud with the cloth of silver and say, in the tongue you have of theirs, that a full weight buys empty benches. The chief thinks about it for the length of the weighing. Then he has them put ashore, every one who was taken on this river. The families find six hundred and fifty pennies for you somehow. The dealer's kinsman, who interpreted where your words ran out, says he will keep your goods at Sliesthorp any summer you like.

He has thought about it for three years and says it in one breath: his Hildswith for your heir, nine hundred pennies with her, and the two houses to stand surety for each other's roofs. She is asked. She says she has counted the days on a longer belt this time.

You pay what is asked and not a penny over. Then you spend the season carrying bread and ale down the Lek in the dark, mast down, to a town that has credit and no coin. It comes to six hundred pennies by the first frost. You could now take that river blind, and some nights you did.
A new river
Your looms and scales stand under a hired roof on the IJssel. A boat from the Rhine ties up beside yours, and her skipper tells the bank what this summer cost Dorestad.

They took the island and killed the count, and then they came up to us and did not even trouble to burn. They put a cloth on the dam and we filled it. The emperor is at Nijmegen asking whose fault it is.
They still say on the dams that you were the first to go. They say it differently this year. What do they ask for a roof here?

There is ground by Saint Lebuin's church, dry four years in five. I pace it out, the priest blesses it, and you pay the church a penny a year for ever. It is not the Rhine. Nothing that comes up it is in a hurry.
The Saxons burned this church twice in my grandfather's time. So you need not tell me about leaving. Tell me what you weigh with, and whether your pennies are the heavy ones.
Wine and cloth that would not sell on the dams at any price are dear here, and dearer since the news: every buyer upriver has understood where the stock is going to be.
Sell the stock while it is dear and take ground of your own by the church
Keep the house afloat: sell dear, and leave a sworn man here with the scales and a hired roof
Take two plots side by side, and send the boat back down for Thiadlef's household

The stock goes for seven hundred pennies, and the ground is paced out before the ink of the tally is dry: eighteen paces of bank, a penny a year to Saint Lebuin. You cut the house's mark on the corner post. It is the same mark. It looks strange on new wood.

You sell for nine hundred and build nothing. A man you trust stays under the hired roof with the second scales and a tally of what is his to sell. The house is where its boat is, as it always was, and now it has a door on two rivers.

The boat goes down empty and comes back with Thiadlef in the bow, his household behind him, and his father's door laid across the thwarts. He says nothing for a day. Then he says the posts here are good oak, and that between two houses there is eleven hundred pennies' worth of stock and one boat too many. He proposes to sail the other one himself.
What is in the ground
The posts of your storehouse stand black to the height of a man. This summer the fleet took silver instead of fire, and the houses that kept their stock short have kept their roofs as well.
The chest is under its alder at De Heul, a spade's depth down, where you put it before you filled the store. It is the only thing you did that summer that you would do again.
You asked me once about the dam head. I said, after the next one. There have been three. Name a price and do not make me say it is too low.
I have a roof and half a store's worth of nothing to put under it. You have stock in your head and no roof. I have seen worse matches made in church.
And there is the matter of the third ship. I would be glad to stop owing you. Put your mark on my door and we will call it paid, and I will go on resenting you in comfort.
In the ash where the counting table stood there is a lump of bronze that was a pair of pans, and beside it, baked hard as a brick, the clay box with the weights still in it.
Dig up the chest and buy the widow's dam head at the price she is frightened enough to take
Dig up the chest and build one roof with Thiadlef on his dam: two marks on one door
Dig up the chest, rake the ashes for the house's scales and its stick of names, and build small

She takes the first price you name, which tells you what it was worth. Forty paces of oak post to deep water, and seven hundred and fifty pennies still in the chest. The bank wants timber for a year to come and you have the berth to land it. People are polite about how you got it.

Your mark goes on his door under his father's, and his steersman stops calling you 'the neighbour'. Seven hundred pennies from the chest go into one stock under one roof. He will take the second boat himself, he says, since somebody in this house ought to know what he is doing.

The weights have come through the fire true: you try them against the moneyer's and he cannot fault them. The pans you have beaten out again, a little crooked. With nine hundred pennies from the ground you roof a store half the size of the old one. The scales hang by the door. Your heirs will be told why they are that shape.
A fleet of the Danes is in Frisia, forty hulls or near it, and has burned on the coast. A fisherman who saw it says they asked the way up the Rhine.
This year the heathen men came by Traiectum to Dorestad and plundered it. Some they killed, some they carried off, and part of the place they burned. The people taken are sold at Sliesthorp.
King Horik of the Danes says the fleets on the Rhine are none of his. Dorestad cloth is sold on his landing all the same, and Dorestad people beside it.
The emperor has ordered guards set along the coasts against the Northmen. The counts who are to keep them are away with their men.
A fleet is on the Maas. Witla has burned, and the fort at Andoverpis on the Scheldt. They will be on the Rhine next.
This year the heathen men took Walcheren and killed its count. At Dorestad they found a bank and a shut gate, lay two days before it, and went away with nothing.
This year the heathen men took Walcheren, killed its count, and took tribute there and at Dorestad. The emperor came to Nijmegen, found the coast unkept, and ordered ships built.
A house of Dorestad has taken ground by Saint Lebuin's church at Daventre and sells Rhine wine there. They say it will not be the last.

A river landing in the delta, a bright windy noon in early summer: a sunburned Frisian fisherman in a salt-stiff hooded cloak sits on the gunwale of a small clinker boat, blistered hands open on his knees, talking up at a merchant; behind them casks are rolled along a wattle dam and nobody is listening.

Dorestad from the river, afternoon sun: the long comb of earth-and-wattle dams with thatched storehouses on them and no wall anywhere; in front a Frankish agent with a tally stick, a thick grey Frisian skipper in a shabby blue cloak laughing, and a thin tonsured priest standing a little apart, listening.

The bank road at Dorestad, dusk, a red sky upriver: a barefoot boy running toward us, mouth open; people throwing bolts of cloth into overloaded boats between the dams; on one dam head a heavy grey man with a short sword stands with a dozen men and spears, not moving.

Dorestad, a grey still morning after the fire: black posts where three storehouses stood, thin smoke, a boat coming back full of women and children; in front a grey skipper stares at the river with a child's shoe in his hand, and a young widow sits on a mooring post with her keys in her lap.

The landing at Sliesthorp, flat northern light, low thatched houses and beached ships: a fair-bearded Dane holds up a bolt of grey-blue cloth with a lead seal dangling from it; behind him on a bench five captives, among them a Frisian girl of fourteen sitting very straight, fingering knots in her belt; a king's man with a spear and an arm ring looks on.

Thiadlef's dam head at Dorestad, evening, new yellow thatch on a mended store: the heavy grey skipper kneels on the planks holding his daughter by both shoulders; she is showing him the knots in her belt; the merchant's boat is still being made fast behind them.

Inside the timber church of Saint Martin at Dorestad, daylight through the open door: twenty merchants standing, a priest scratching a line of ditch and bank on the earth floor with a stick, a grey skipper spreading a cloth as if laying out silver, a Frankish agent with folded arms; through the door a barge loading a loom.

The gatehouse of the palace at Noviomagus on its hill above the Waal, a cool clear morning: a young tonsured clerk at a sloping desk with a wax seal and a strip of parchment, an empty courtyard behind him; through the gate, far below, stacked oak trunks on the river bank and a small boat.

The sea off the Maas mouth, hazy afternoon, low dunes along the horizon: a line of more than twenty square sails standing in toward the land; one long ship has turned and rows toward us, shields along her side, a man standing in her bow with a hand raised; in the foreground the stern of a small trading boat with ale casks.

Dorestad from the bank road, a hot hazy day: a raw earth bank chest-high with a ditch in front and a gap where the road goes through, men digging; a merchant selling wine casks cheap on a dam while looking downstream; boats with bedding aboard at every dam head.

Dawn mist on the river below Dorestad: a ditch, a raw earth bank topped with a wattle fence, and a shut two-leaved oak gate with a watch-house and a man blowing a horn; spearmen along the bank, among them a heavy grey skipper; on the water twenty long ships lying on their oars, one small boat rowing back to them.

A dam head at Dorestad, noon, no smoke: a cloth spread on the planks heaped with pennies and cut silver, a pair of scales held by a Danish chief with gold arm rings, Frisian merchants standing in a silent half circle; behind him a long ship with captives sitting among the rowers; an unfinished bank in the far background.

The bank of the IJssel at Daventre, a mild evening: a small timber church with a shingled roof, a man pacing out ground with a measuring pole, looms and a pair of scales under an open lean-to; two Frisian boats side by side at the bank, a skipper telling news with his hands.

A burned plot on a dam at Dorestad, clear cold morning: black posts standing man-high in grey ash, a merchant kneeling and lifting a warped bronze scale pan out of it; a widow with keys at her belt and a heavy grey skipper wait at the edge of the ash; whole roofs on either side.
Ending picture, the bank holds: a shut oak gate in an earth bank at dawn, a horn hanging beside it, and beyond the bank the masts of long ships going away down a misty river.
Ending picture, the tribute of 837: a cloth heaped with silver pennies on the planks of a dam, a pair of scales standing in it, and a long ship's prow above.
Ending picture, up the river: a river barge loaded with a loom, a house door and a cat, going upstream under a grey sky, with a thin smoke far astern.
Ending picture, the storehouse in ashes: a bent pair of bronze scale pans and a box of weights lying in ash between black posts, and beside them a spade and a small iron-bound chest with earth on it.
